muc.title: What does AI actually learn?
muc.text: Everyone says AI is "trained". But when AI learns, what actually changes inside it? The answer: billions of tiny knobs.

muc.title: Go out for coffee?
muc.text: Picture a small decision: should I go out for coffee this afternoon? You think about three things: is it raining, did a friend invite you, and do you have money left?

muc.title: One knob for each thing
muc.text: Each thing has its own knob, called a weight. A friend's invite pushes hard toward "go", rain pulls the other way. Add them all up, and if it passes a threshold, you decide: go.

muc.title: An artificial neuron
muc.text: That is an artificial neuron: it takes a few numbers, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, then decides. Surprisingly simple.

muc.title: Stacked into layers
muc.text: Stack thousands of neurons into layers, each layer passing its results to the next, and you have a neural network. The first layer spots lines, the middle layers spot ears and eyes, and the last layer says: cat.

muc.title: Learning means turning the knobs itself
muc.text: Big chatbots have hundreds of billions of these knobs, and nobody turns them by hand. "Learning" means the machine turns each knob itself, a little at a time, until it gets the right answer.

muc.title: Watch the knobs turn themselves
muc.text: Want to see it for yourself? Open playground.tensorflow.org, press play, and watch the connecting lines get darker and lighter. Those are the knobs turning themselves.

muc.title: Which knob, which way?
muc.text: But how does the machine know which knob to turn, and which way? First, it has to know how wrong it is. See you in part 2.
